m.s: The First National Day of Thanksgiving, 1789
o: God of all grace, I rise today with a heart full of gratitude. Thank you for life, for the air I breathe, for the roof that shelters me, and for the people who walk with me. So often I ask for more before thanking you for what you have already given, and today I want to reverse the order: first I thank you, then I ask.

Lord, thank you for the victory you give us through our Lord Jesus Christ. Thank you, because our labor in you is not in vain, even when we do not always see its fruits. Thank you for the indescribable gift, your Son, who gave himself for us. My list of blessings is long, even if on hard days I forget it. Remind me of it today, and make me a grateful witness before others.

Help me to be firm and steady in what you have entrusted to me. May I not admit defeat to weariness or let complaining master me. Give me eyes to see goodness in the everyday: bread, health, unexpected help, a child's laughter. Teach me to share what I have with those in need, and to say a word of appreciation to those who serve me. May my gratitude be seen in my actions and not only on my lips. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 26, 1789, the people of the newly formed United States were invited to celebrate a national day of thanksgiving to God. President George Washington had proclaimed it on October 3 of that year, in New York, after both houses of Congress asked him to. The date set was Thursday, November 26.

The proclamation asked that the day be devoted to thanking almighty God for his many blessings. It mentioned how God had cared for the people before they were a nation, the opportunity to establish a peaceful form of government, and the freedom to practice religion. It was a solemn document, written by a young country that had just come out of a difficult war.

One detail deserves attention. The text did not merely give thanks; it also asked God's forgiveness for the nation's faults and prayed that he would help those who governed to fulfill their duties justly. Thus gratitude came with humility. It was not thanks given with pride, like someone congratulating himself, but with the recognition that every good thing comes from above.

The Bible has always joined gratitude with faith. The Psalms are full of songs of thanksgiving, and Paul wrote words of thanks to the Corinthians for the victory in Christ. A day of national gratitude is a good occasion to remember something more personal: every home and every heart can have its own day of thanksgiving, today, without waiting for a calendar.
m.c: May the God of all goodness be with you every hour of this day and remind you of his blessings. Go out with a steady step, knowing that he knows your needs and cares for you. His faithfulness surrounds you, and your hope in him will not be disappointed.
m: Gratitude is not a feeling that appears only when everything is going well. It is a decision that is practiced, and the Bible presents it as part of a steadfast life. Paul ends his great teaching on the resurrection with a sentence that invites thanksgiving: thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Notice what follows. Paul does not stop at applause, but adds a very practical application: be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain. Gratitude sustains us in routine. Whoever gives thanks finds strength to keep serving even when no one notices.

In his second letter, Paul speaks of God's indescribable gift. With that expression he sums up what we can neither pay for nor fully explain: the gift of Jesus. If we receive something so great without deserving it, the natural response is a grateful and generous heart. The Providence that cared for a young nation is the same that sustains your family today.

I suggest a practice for today. At the start of the morning, name out loud five concrete blessings, without repeating yesterday's. During the day, thank three people for something specific they did for you. When a difficulty comes, before complaining, say: Lord, thank you that even in this you are with me. You will see your spirits change, and gratitude open up space for peace.

t.s: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
o: Good Father, at the end of this day I want to thank you for everything I have received from your hand. Thank you for food, for work, for conversations, for moments of laughter, and also for lessons that came disguised as difficulties. I recognize that nothing I have is only mine, for it is you who gave it to me.

Lord Jesus, as you took the loaves from that young boy and gave thanks before distributing them, teach me to place in your hands the little I have. Sometimes I feel that my time, my strength, and my resources are not enough. Today I give them to you again, convinced that in your hands what is small becomes sufficient. Forgive me if I let pass an opportunity to help someone, and give me the chance to do so tomorrow.

I pray for those who will go to bed tonight with hunger, loneliness, or fear. May bread and hope not be lacking for them, and use my hands, if you wish, to bring them some relief. I give you what has been left unresolved, for you gather even the pieces that remain, and nothing is lost with you. Grant me restful sleep and a calm heart. Thank you for your faithfulness that never fails. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: The Gospel of John tells how a great crowd followed Jesus beside the Sea of Galilee, because they saw the signs he performed on the sick. When it grew late, Jesus looked at the crowd and asked Philip where they could buy bread for them to eat. He did it to test him, for he already knew what he was going to do.

Philip answered with numbers: even two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each to have a little. Then Andrew, another disciple, pointed out that there was a boy there who had five barley loaves and two small fish. And he added an honest question: what are these for so many people? It was little, and the disciples knew it.

Jesus ordered the people to sit down on the grass. There were about five thousand men. Then he took the loaves, gave thanks, and distributed them, and did the same with the fish, as much as they wanted. Notice the order: first gratitude, then the miracle. Jesus did not wait to have more before giving thanks; he gave thanks for what there was.

When all were satisfied, Jesus asked that the leftover pieces be gathered, so that nothing would be lost. They filled twelve baskets with the pieces from the five barley loaves. The message is comforting: the little handed over to Jesus does not merely suffice; there is some left over. And God's care extends even to what others would let be thrown away.
t.c: Rest now in the certainty that the Lord has cared for every detail of your day, even those you did not notice. Give thanks, let go of what weighs on you, and let his peace cover you. Sleep soundly, for the God who provides will keep providing tomorrow.
m: The story of the boy with the five loaves holds a special lesson for evenings of gratitude. Often we end the day thinking about what was lacking: time, money, energy, patience. Andrew did the same when he asked what five loaves and two fish were for so many people. His question was sincere, but Jesus had another way of seeing scarcity.

Jesus took the little, gave thanks, and distributed it. See how much happens in that gesture. There was someone who agreed to give up his meal. There was a Master who gave thanks before seeing the result. And there were disciples who served the crowd with their own hands. This is how God works: he uses our small offering and fills it with his power, so that it is enough for all.

Tonight, instead of counting what you could not do, take an inventory of what you placed in God's hands. A kind word, a simple service, a task finished honestly. All of it counts. And what you feel was not enough, you can hand to the Lord now, like those barley loaves. He knows how to multiply it in his time.

Notice also the twelve baskets of leftovers. God does not merely meet the need; he takes care of what remains. This speaks of a generous and orderly Father, who wastes nothing of what we give him. Before you sleep, give thanks for one concrete thing you received today, and think of someone with whom you could share something tomorrow. Gratitude grows when it is shared.
